title: Paper Explained: When No Benchmark Exists: Validating Comparative LLM Safety Scoring Without Ground-Truth Labels - A Beginner's Guide
subtitle: AI Safety Without Labels: A New Scoring Method

content.background:
Before this work, experts often relied on labeled examples to judge how safe a language model is. But in many real-world cases—different languages, new sectors, or new rules—there aren’t reliable “ground-truth” labels telling you what the safe output should look like. Without those labels, it’s hard to say which model is safer in a principled way. It’s like trying to pick the safest car to buy when there are no crash-test results for that car in the city you’ll drive it in. In practice, gathering perfect labels is expensive, time-consuming, or even inappropriate, so people end up comparing models with shaky or incomplete evidence.

Even when you do run safety tests, the results can be fragile. The score you get depends on many choices: which safety scenarios you test (the kinds of situations you imagine), who does the testing, how you phrase prompts, how many times you rerun tests, and what you decide counts as “safe.” Without ground-truth labels, a single number can hide important variability—for example, a model seeming safer only for one kind of scenario or because of testing bias. The paper shows that in real evaluations, the “best model” can change based on these setup choices, so using a single ranking to drive deployment decisions can be misleading. They also demonstrate this with a Norwegian safety package, where the apparent safety of a model shifted with scenario category and risk measure.

This gives the motivation for the work: in public sector and regulated contexts, decisions about which model to deploy must be backed by trustworthy evidence, not just a single score. If the evaluation setup itself differs, you’re not really comparing apples to apples. The research aims to formalize how to interpret scenario-based audits as deployment evidence when there are no ground-truth labels, and to emphasize that the full testing context—what scenarios, who audits, how samples are chosen, and how many reruns are done—needs to be reported. In short, it addresses a practical gap between how we test safety in the lab and how we justify safe deployments in the real world.
content.methodology:
Here’s the core idea in beginner-friendly terms. When there isn’t a labeled dataset telling you which model is “safer,” you can’t just rank models by a ground-truth score. The paper tackles this by turning safety evaluation into a fixed, contract-based audit. You agree in advance on a scenario pack (the set of test situations), a scoring rubric, who audits and who judges, how you sample cases, and how many reruns you’re allowed. Then you run a controlled, scenario-by-scenario comparison and interpret the results as deployment evidence rather than a single universal label. The key twist is to replace ground-truth labels with an instrumental validity idea: you check whether the scoring responds to deliberate safety manipulations, whether the target-driven differences dominate over reviewer quirks, and whether results stay stable across repeated runs.

How they do it, conceptually, in steps:
- Fix the evaluation contract: decide the scenario pack, rubric, who is the auditor and judge, how you sample, and how many reruns you’ll allow.
- Build an instrumental validity chain: introduce safe-versus-ablated contrasts (controlled safety manipulations) to see if the scoring truly tracks safety, not just reader bias or random noise.
- Use a local scoring instrument (SimpleAudit) to run the benchmarkless comparison on the chosen safety pack (in the study, a Norwegian safety pack) and collect scores.
- Examine what drives the scores: check that the model’s response changes mainly because of the safety manipulation (target-driven effects) rather than artifacts from auditors or judges, and test whether results hold up after multiple reruns.
- Cross-check with another tool (Petri) to see if the same chain yields consistent conclusions, showing the idea isn’t tied to a single instrument.
- Apply it to a real-world procurement case (Borealis vs Gemma 3) to show how results can shift depending on scenario category and risk measure, underlining that you should report a full evidence package rather than a single ranking.

What this buys you and how to read the results conceptually:
- Without a ground-truth label, you don’t claim one model is definitively “safer.” Instead, you present a structured set of evidence that the safety scoring is meaningful within a defined deployment context.
- The study finds that a strong safety signal can be detected (high discrimination between safe and ablated targets), that a large portion of the variation in scores is driven by the target identity (the safety manipulation you injected), and that the results become more stable after several reruns.
- When they tried a different tool, the same chain could work, but the differences you see sit upstream of the scoring itself—what contract you enforce, and how you expect deployment to fit the scenario. In a real procurement example, this mattered: safer choices depended on which scenario category you’re evaluating and which risk measure you care about.
- The practical takeaway is clear: you should report the full evidence package—scores, how big the deltas are, uncertainty, and the specific auditors and judges involved—rather than collapsing everything into a single rank. This makes the evaluation transpare nt and decisions traceable to the deployment context.

In short, the paper proposes a principled way to compare LLM safety without labels by building a disciplined, scenario-grounded audit. It shows that safety assessments are inherently contextual and that the value of the evidence comes from how well the scoring chain is constructed, how stable it is across reruns, and how clearly you report the full set of results and the deployment context.
content.results:
This paper tackles a real problem: how can we compare the safety of different language models when there isn’t a ready-made benchmark with ground-truth labels to tell us which one is safer? The authors propose a practical way to do this called benchmarkless comparative safety scoring. They formalize a process they call a scenario-based audit, surrounded by a contract that specifies what counts as the evaluation scenario, the scoring rubric, who acts as the auditor and judge, how samples are drawn, and how many re-runs are allowed. Because there are no labels to trust, they replace ground-truth checks with an “instrumental-validity chain”—a way to show that the scoring actually responds to safe-vs-harm contrasts, that the model being tested is the main source of variation (not the judges or auditors), and that results stay stable across multiple tries. This gives a principled, repeatable way to turn an audit into deployment evidence.

The authors implement this idea in a tool called SimpleAudit and test it in real-world-like settings. They show that when comparing safe content to ablated (safety-reduced) content, the method can clearly distinguish the two, and that the identity of the target model is the biggest driver of differences, with results stabilizing after a handful of reruns. They also apply the same chain to another tool (Petri) and find that the approach works there too, but the differences you see start upstream—how the evaluation contract is written and how well the tool fits a given deployment. In a Norwegian public-sector procurement case comparing two models (Borealis and Gemma 3), they illustrate that which model appears safer actually depends on the scenario category and the risk measure you care about. The key takeaway is that safety scores aren’t a single number; you must report multiple pieces of information—scores, how deltas look, uncertainty, and details about who audited and judged the evaluation—so that decisions reflect the true context.

Practically, this work is significant because it gives a concrete way to compare safety in new domains where labeled benchmarks don’t exist. It moves the field beyond chasing a single ranking to embracing a richer, more transparent summary of evidence. By showing how to validate scoring through a controlled contrast, how to ensure results aren’t just the tester’s biases, and how results can vary with deployment context, the paper offers a usable path for researchers and policymakers to make safer deployment decisions. The emphasis on reporting multiple factors and the explicit role of the evaluation contract are among the key breakthroughs, aiming for results that are reliable, reproducible, and actionable in real-world procurement and deployment.
content.significance:
This paper matters today because it tackles a realistic problem: in many new AI areas there isn’t a labeled “ground truth” to tell you which model is safer. Instead of chasing a single score, the authors propose a scaffolded, scenario-driven way to judge safety. They show that you can still make credible deployment decisions by using a fixed set of scenarios, a clear rubric, and an audit trail, even when you don’t have true-positive/true-negative labels. The idea of testing a model’s safety response to controlled contrasts, checking how much of the signal comes from the target model vs. the auditors, and watching stability across repeated runs gives you a disciplined, repeatable way to compare models in real-world contexts.

In the long run, this work helped push AI safety evaluation away from “one number fits all” towards context-aware, evidence-based decision making. It highlights that safety scores are not universal truths but tools that depend on the scenario category, risk measure, and deployment fit. The paper’s emphasis on reporting all parts of the evaluation—scores, deltas, uncertainty, and who did the judging—also foreshadows a broader shift toward transparent, auditable risk assessments in AI. You can see this lineage in later safety toolchains and governance work that favor multi-metric dashboards, scenario packs, and explicit contract-like conditions for deployment, rather than blanket rankings.

For modern systems people use every day, like ChatGPT and other large-language models, the message is highly practical: safety is task- and context-specific. The paper shows concrete tools and concepts, such as SimpleAudit and Petri, plus a real-world procurement example (a Norwegian case comparing Borealis and Gemma 3), that illustrate how safety evaluation can play a concrete role in choosing and deploying models. Today, this translates to how organizations evaluate AI in different domains (customer support, healthcare, finance) with scenario-based tests, publish how results depend on the test setup, and require transparency about which evaluator, which scenario, and which risk metric produced which result. In short, the paper’s lasting impact is a clearer, more accountable way to talk about AI safety in the wild—important for researchers, policymakers, and anyone deciding which AI to adopt in real products.

concept_explanation.title: Understanding Instrumental Validity Chain: The Heart of When No Benchmark Exists
concept_explanation.content:
Imagine you’re judging how safely different cars drive in a new city where there are no official crash-test labels for those cars yet. You can’t just give one number like “safest” because you don’t have ground-truth labels. Instead, you run a careful, repeatable judging method: you pick a fixed set of driving scenarios (scenario pack), a clear rubric for scoring safety, a panel of judges, an auditing step to check consistency, and you decide how many test runs you’ll do. The paper’s “instrumental validity chain” is exactly that: a series of checks to make sure the scoring tool is actually measuring safety in a trustworthy way, given the context and rules you’ve set.

Here’s how it works, step by step. First, you define the evaluation setup: a scenario pack (the kinds of prompts or situations you test), a rubric (how you rate safety), who the auditors are, who the judges are, how you sample prompts, and how many reruns you allow. Then you create a controlled contrast you can manipulate, like a safe version of a prompt versus an ablated version where safety constraints are weakened. You look to see if the model’s safety scores respond to this contrast in a meaningful way—think of it as testing whether the scoring is really capturing safety, not just random noise. You quantify this responsiveness with a metric called AUROC (how well the safe vs. unsafe versions separate in scores); in the paper they report values between 0.89 and 1.00, which means the system reliably tells apart safe from unsafe under their setup.

Next, you check where the variation in the scores comes from. The “instrumental validity chain” wants the variation due to the model’s true safety signal (the target-driven variance) to dominate over artifacts from the auditors or judges. In practice, you measure how much of the score changes are due to the model’s behavior versus who is judging or how you sampled prompts. A useful statistic they report is eta-squared (η^2); in their Norwegian safety tests, the target identity variance was about 0.52, meaning the model’s safety signal is the main driver of differences, not the judges’ moods or the random quirks of the setup. Finally, you test stability by rerunning the same scoring plan several times (they find stability after about ten reruns for certain severity profiles). If these conditions hold, the scores can be treated as valid evidence under the defined scenario pack and contract.

Why does this matter? Because in the real world, you often must compare safety across language models without any labeled ground truth. The instrumental validity chain gives you a disciplined way to claim that your scoring evidence is trustworthy within a specific, well-documented context. The paper shows how this works in practice with SimpleAudit (a local-first scoring tool) and Petri (another tool), and it even Flags that the same chain can yield different conclusions when you change upstream decisions like how you enforce claims in the contract or how you plan deployment. For example, in a Norwegian public-sector procurement case comparing Borealis and Gemma 3, the “safer” model wasn’t the same across all scenario categories or risk measures. That means you should report not just a single ranking, but the scores, how much deltas vary, where critical rates lie, the uncertainty, and exactly which auditor and judge were involved. Practically, this leads to more careful, transparent decision-making in AI safety, especially in regulated or high-stakes contexts.

For students and practitioners, the take-home is simple: when labels aren’t available, you can still build trustworthy comparisons by making the evaluation framework explicit and by checking three things in sequence—the model’s true safety signal in response to controlled contrasts, the dominance of that signal over evaluation artifacts, and the stability of results across repeated runs. This approach helps you design safer AI systems, design better audits, and communicate results clearly to stakeholders. A practical checklist you could use includes: define the scenario pack and rubric clearly, implement a controlled safe-vs-ablated contrast, quantify target-driven versus artifact variance, run enough reruns to test stability, and report all components (scores, deltas, uncertainty, and who audited) instead of compressing everything into a single ranking.

summary: This paper introduces a formal framework and a practical tool (SimpleAudit) for benchmarkless safety scoring that uses an instrumental-validity chain to turn scenario-based audits into deployment evidence when no ground-truth labels exist, showing that scores, uncertainties, and the audit setup must be reported together rather than collapsed into a single ranking.
